target.title: fix(ai): normalize non-conforming tool-call ids reaching Anthropic/Google targets (#95623)
target.body:
Fixes #95623

## What Problem This Solves

After a cross-provider failover, an OpenAI-responses composite tool-call id (`call_XXX|fc_YYY`) can reach an **Anthropic** target still containing the `|`. Anthropic requires tool ids matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, so it hard-400s the whole replay and the session is bricked for its own primary provider — no new turns without a reset.

This happens on two paths that the existing `#61254` sanitizer misses:
- **Orphaned tool result** — the paired tool call was dropped (compaction/windowing), so there is no in-pass map entry and the raw id passes through untouched.
- **Same-model-tagged call** — a failover-introduced id whose provenance looks same-model as the Anthropic target skips normalization (`!isSameModel` guard), so both the call and its result keep the `|`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`packages/ai/src/providers/transform-messages.ts` owns cross-provider tool-call-id normalization but only normalized `toolCall` ids when `!isSameModel`, and `toolResult` ids only via an in-pass `toolCallIdMap`. Non-conforming ids leaked through both gaps.

A blanket "always normalize" is unsafe: the OpenAI-completions/OpenAI-responses/Mistral normalizers are **not idempotent** on their own native ids (openai-completions strips the `|fc_…` half; openai-responses reads the `source` message; mistral is a stateful id map), so applying them to same-model native ids would corrupt valid replays.

So `transformMessages` gains an opt-in `targetSafeToolCallIds` flag, passed `true` only by the **Anthropic and Google** call sites whose normalizers are charset scrubs that are idempotent on their native ids. In target-safe mode every tool id reaching the target is normalized — the same-model call and the map-miss result included — and because the scrub is deterministic, a call and its result stay paired. Every other provider keeps the default (`false`), so their behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged.

The shared transform owns this invariant, so the fix stays there (not at the Anthropic transport-serialization boundary, which cannot see the shared call/result pairing). Non-goals: no change to any provider's normalizer semantics, no change to cross-provider behavior, and no id-collision hashing.

## User Impact

Sessions that fail over to an OpenAI-responses model and later replay to an Anthropic primary no longer brick on an Anthropic 400 — the foreign composite id is scrubbed to a conforming id (`call_XXX_fc_YYY`) on both the call and its result. Google targets get the same protection. OpenAI/Mistral users are unaffected.

## Evidence

Real behavior via the actual `transformMessages` (Anthropic target, composite id `call_AbCd0123|fc_beef01`), head `e7e315d6c5a3`:

~~~text
AFTER S1-safe orphan (targetSafe=true):          ["result:call_AbCd0123_fc_beef01"]                                | PIPE-SURVIVES=false
AFTER S3-safe same-model-mistag (targetSafe=true): ["call:call_AbCd0123_fc_beef01","result:call_AbCd0123_fc_beef01"] | PIPE-SURVIVES=false
REGRESSION default (targetSafe=false) same-model:  ["call:call_AbCd0123|fc_beef01","result:call_AbCd0123|fc_beef01"] | PIPE-SURVIVES=true
~~~

The two target-safe paths scrub the `|`; the default path leaves a same-model id byte-for-byte untouched (proving no OpenAI/Mistral corruption). On current `main` (target-safe absent) both S1 and S3 leak — `PIPE-SURVIVES=true`.

- `vitest run packages/ai/src/providers/transform-messages.test.ts` — 5 passed (2 red-first #95623 guards for S1/S3 + 3 regressions: default-mode composite untouched, cross-provider pair still mapped, source-requiring normalizer never invoked on a map-miss result).
- Negative control: with the source fix stashed, the S1 & S3 guard tests fail (`expected 'call_AbCd0123|fc_beef01' to be 'call_AbCd0123_fc_beef01'`) — confirms the tests guard the bug.
- Broader regression: all `packages/ai/src/providers` tests — 356 passed; the 1 failure (`openai-chatgpt-responses` zstd-SSE encoding) reproduces identically with my change stashed, i.e. pre-existing/unrelated (a zstd env issue on this host).
- `tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json` / `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json` — no errors; `oxfmt --check` — clean; `check:loc` — passes (all growth in the sub-500-line transform; the three oversized provider files stay net-zero).

## Notes

- Distinct from #95671 (guarded only the same-model path at the transport-serialization boundary, missing orphan results) and #95629 — this fixes both leak paths at the owning transform boundary with zero cross-provider regression.
- AI-assisted (Claude Code); I have reviewed and understand every line.

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Some deployments serve a Claude/MiniMax model through a proxy that intermittently degrades a native `tool_use` block into plain text. In that degraded case the tool call arrives as the namespaced/bare XML attribute dialect — `<invoke name="tool"><parameter name="x">v</parameter></invoke>`, optionally wrapped in `<function_calls>...</function_calls>` and optionally prefixed with `antml:` or `mm:`.

On current `main` two gaps remained:

1. The visible-text sanitizer recognized the `antml:` prefix but not the `mm:` prefix, so a degraded `mm:invoke` block leaked verbatim into the user-visible reply.
2. The persist-path stripper (`packages/tool-call-repair` `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks`) did not recognize the attribute-dialect invoke at all, so an unfenced standalone degraded invoke block was written into the durable `done.message` instead of being scrubbed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user, and it must not be persisted into session state either — but a legitimate code example of the same markup (inside a fenced or inline code span) must be preserved, not deleted. This change teaches both layers about the full attribute dialect using a closed `(?:antml:|mm:)?` namespace allow-list, so arbitrary `ns:` tokens in prose are never matched.

This PR was re-implemented on top of current `main` after upstream refactored the tool-call-repair package (the new `scanXmlishToolCall` seam and code-region helpers). The change is scoped to the net delta that still reproduces on `main`:

- **Visible text** (`assistant-visible-text.ts`): mirror the existing `antml:` handling for the `mm:` namespace in the tag-name scan, quick-check, and payload-start patterns. The `<function_calls>`-wrapped bare-invoke case is already scrubbed by the package strip stage in the delivery pipeline.
- **Persist path** (`packages/tool-call-repair`): a dedicated linear scanner recognizes a complete standalone invoke block (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `<function_calls>` wrapper, self-closing, and zero-parameter forms). The scanner returns `none`/`incomplete`/`complete`, so on an unterminated open the strip loop bails and preserves the remainder — exactly mirroring the existing dialects — keeping the scan linear on adversarial input.
- **Code-region awareness**: the strip takes an optional code-region predicate evaluated at the block's start offset. Fenced/inline Markdown examples of the invoke dialect are preserved while unfenced standalone leaked blocks are scrubbed. Without a predicate the package strip lazily computes code regions so a bare call still spares examples.
- **Plugin SDK contract preserved**: the exported `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it forces a scrub of every region, even inside code, for untrusted callers), with code-aware behavior available only via the explicit `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` opt-in.
- **Layering**: `findCodeRegions`/`isInsideCode`/`CodeRegion` were moved into `normalization-core` (the package's only dependency) so `tool-call-repair` can share one implementation without importing app source; `src/shared/text/code-regions.ts` re-exports them so existing callers are unaffected.

Non-goals/boundaries: the native Anthropic/DSML transports are untouched; no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced; the equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged; the invoke dialect is recognized only by the strip/sanitize paths (never promoted to an executable call and never wired into the stream-buffering scanner).

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude/MiniMax routes no longer see raw namespaced/bare `invoke` tool-call XML in their replies, and the leaked block is no longer written into the persisted message (no session-state content loss). Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped. A resolved-review audit also removed an O(n²) worst case on the persist strip path, so adversarial degraded text cannot cause pathological CPU use.

## Evidence

Focused regression tests were added at the layers that own the contract:
- `packages/tool-call-repair/src/payload.test.ts`: invoke-dialect variants (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `function_calls` wrapper, self-closing, zero-param), code-region preservation vs. unfenced scrub, the predicate override, and a linear-time guard against many unterminated opens.
- `src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts`: the `preserveCodeRegions` opt-in and strict default.
- `src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts`: the `mm:invoke`/`mm:parameter` visible-text case (parallel to the existing `antml:` case), alongside existing standalone-vs-inline `function_calls` delivery-path coverage.

Real-behavior proof (before = current `main`, after = this branch), driving the actual `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` and `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` on the leak shapes:

```
=== BEFORE (main) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it.\n<mm:invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<mm:parameter name=\"city\">Paris</mm:parameter>\n</mm:invoke>"
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done.\n<function_calls>\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>\n</function_calls>"
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (preserved)

=== AFTER (this branch) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it."
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done."
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (still preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (still preserved)
```

The three real leak shapes (A2 visible `mm:`, A3 visible `function_calls`-wrapped bare invoke, C1 persisted unfenced standalone invoke) are now scrubbed, while the fenced (B1) and inline (B2) code examples remain untouched — the exact over-scrub concern is verified closed.

O(n²) audit fix: a resolved-review pass measured the persist strip degrading quadratically on adversarial input with many unterminated invoke opens (720 KB ≈ 977 ms, scaling to seconds for a few MB). Making the scanner bail on `incomplete` (mirroring the existing unterminated-candidate bail) brought the same 720 KB input to ≈ 0.8 ms and restored linear scaling; a regression test locks this.

Verification: `tool-call-repair` grammar/payload/stream-normalizer (157 passed), `provider-stream-shared` + `tool-payload` + `assistant-visible-text` + `sanitize-text` + `message-action-runner.send-validation` + `embedded-agent-utils` (all green), `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` exit 0, `plugin-sdk:api:check` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` exit 0 (surface budget bumped by the one new `StripPlainTextToolCallOptions` type), oxfmt clean, `git diff --check` clean. Rebased onto current `main` (`9b823c61`).

target.title: fix(media-understanding): apply image compression policy to media:// references
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: media:// image references, explicit model calls, and CLI infer image describe all bypassed image compression policy, causing oversized photos to fail with provider dimension limit errors
- Solution: Resolve image compression policy from two sources — configured model metadata (openclaw.json) + bundled static catalog — and apply it via optimizeImageBufferForWebMedia before provider execution. Covers all three entry points: channel-triggered media:// references, runtime API describeImageFileWithModel, and CLI infer image describe --model.
- What changed: 6 files (+110/-100 relative to original PR head, +126/-14 net vs main at time of original PR)
  - runner.entries.ts: resolveImageCompressionPolicyFromConfig now merges configured model limits (cfg.models.providers.*.models[].mediaInput.image) with bundled static catalog limits. Configured takes priority; catalog fills gaps.
  - runtime.ts: imports the shared helper from runner.entries; passes provider/model through prepareImageDescriptionInput to resolve model-aware policy
  - capability-cli.ts: passes activeModel.provider/model into prepareImageDescriptionInput so catalog/config limits are resolved for CLI image describe
  - runner.test-mocks.ts: add applySecretRefHeaderSentinels to model-auth mock (upstream compat)
  - runner.vision-skip.test.ts: add media-services.js + provider-secret-egress mocks (upstream compat)
  - apply.test.ts: add createImageProcessor/readImageProbe mocks and adapt HEIC test expectations (upstream compat)
- What did NOT change: image tool (resolveCompressionModelPolicy unchanged), HEIC normalization boundary, web-media helpers, config surface

Fixes #101923

## Root Cause

- resolveImageCompressionPolicyFromConfig only read agents.defaults (preferredSidePx), producing a policy without hard maxSidePx/maxPixels. optimizeImageBufferForWebMedia preserves originals when no hard constraints exist, so provider-specific dimension caps (e.g. Anthropic 2576px maxSidePx) were bypassed.
- The CLI --model path also called preparation before provider/model were known, so the model-catalog lookup could not resolve.
- Missing detection: no test verifying media-understanding applies the same model-aware policy as the image tool.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Oversized images reaching media-understanding providers without compression, bypassing provider dimension caps
- **Real environment tested:** Linux Node 22, pnpm install + pnpm build, worktree isolation
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
```bash
# Generate oversized test image
convert -size 4096x4096 xc:red /tmp/test-oversized-4096.png
# Run integrated pipeline with model-aware policy
```
- **Evidence after fix:**
```
BEFORE: /tmp/test-oversized-4096.png PNG 4096x4096
POLICY: {"quality":"balanced","models":[{"preferredSidePx":2048},{"maxSidePx":2576,"preferredSidePx":2576}]}
AFTER: /tmp/test-optimized.png JPEG 2048x2048
VERDICT: 4096x4096 → 2048x2048 ✅
```
- **Observed result after fix:** 4096x4096 PNG compressed to 2048x2048 JPEG. Policy merges agents.defaults (preferredSidePx:2048) with bundled static catalog mediaInput.image (maxSidePx:2576 from anthropic/claude-sonnet-5) and configured model metadata when present. All three code paths now pass provider/model into compression resolution.
- **What was not tested:** Live provider execution (no API keys). Image processing pipeline and policy resolution validated through unit tests; the compression path reuses the same web-media helpers and catalog lookup the image tool already exercises in live calls.

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage level: Unit tests across media-understanding test files
- Test files and pass counts:
  - runtime.test.ts: 21/21 — image normalization, HEIC bypass, remote references
  - runner.vision-skip.test.ts: 18/18 — provider routing, native vision skip, MiniMax VLM fallback
  - runner.entries.guards.test.ts: 12/12 — entry guard invariants
  - apply.test.ts: 54/54 — attachment transcription, local binary probing, HEIC images
  - image-tool.test.ts: 94/94 — sibling image-tool compression policy contract
  - **Total: 199/199 passing**
- Upstream compat fixes: pre-existing test failures from upstream secret-sentinel changes (RastermillError in vision-skip/apply tests due to missing media-services mocks) are also resolved.

## Risk checklist

- **Backward compatibility:** ✅ optional opts added; callers without provider/model get config-only behavior
- **Config contract:** ✅ reads existing agents.defaults + cfg.models.providers (no new config surface)
- **Provider contracts:** ✅ respects catalog mediaInput.image limits; configured limits take priority
- **HEIC conversion:** ✅ preserved (optimization runs before HEIC normalization)
- **Performance:** ✅ process-stable catalog lookup + config property reads; no async I/O added
- **Side effects:** ✅ only media-understanding image paths
- **Image tool unaffected:** ✅ resolveCompressionModelPolicy unchanged

target.title: feat(gateway): deliver plugin approvals to paired iOS devices via APNs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Exec approvals reach paired iOS operator devices via APNs push, but plugin approvals do not — they only reach chat via the forwarder. So an agent blocked on a plugin approval (for example the `onepassword` broker's `approve` tier) raised no native notification on the operator's phone or watch. This wires plugin approvals into the same APNs delivery, so they raise a native notification on paired iOS devices, which iOS then mirrors to a paired Apple Watch.

Follow-up to the 1Password broker work (#105924). The iOS client change to render the plugin-approval notification/dialog is a separate PR; this is the server half.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Generalized the exec-only iOS push delivery into a shared driver: exec and plugin instances share paired-device resolution, the `operator.approvals` + `operator.read` scope gate, APNs registration loading, direct/relay delivery planning, and stale-registration cleanup. Exec and plugin drivers supply their own APNs senders; the transport/relay/auth logic stays single-sourced.
- Added `plugin.approval.requested` / `plugin.approval.resolved` APNs payloads and a `openclaw.plugin-approval` category. Title comes from the approval request (fallback "Approval required"); body is the request description truncated to 256 UTF-16-safe characters. No secret-bearing fields are added — plugin approval title/description are plugin/operator-authored and never contain the secret value.
- Wired push into both plugin-approval origination points so coverage is complete: the `plugin.approval.request` RPC handler and the `node.invoke` policy path both fan out to the existing chat forwarder plus the new iOS push, using the same `isTargetVisible` predicate exec uses to skip a device already viewing the approval in-app. Resolution and expiry send the same cleanup wake exec does.

No new config surface: native push follows exec's behavior (always enabled for eligible paired operator devices); `approvals.plugin.enabled` remains the chat-forwarding gate.

## User Impact

Operators with a paired iOS device (and optionally a watch) now get a native approval notification for plugin approvals, in addition to the existing chat forward. Opt-in only in the sense that it requires a paired operator device with the approvals scope; no behavior change for setups without one. Exec approval behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Focused tests green: `exec-approval-ios-push` (13), `push-apns` (18), `plugin-approval` (33), `approval` (33), `node-invoke-plugin-policy` (16), `server-request-context` (5), `server-aux-handlers` (12) — covering direct and relay delivery, scope-gate filtering, lifecycle cleanup, and payload construction incl. body truncation and category/kind.
- Production types, test-types (Blacksmith Testbox), and oxlint all exit 0; `git diff --check` clean.
- Autoreview (Codex gpt-5.6-sol xhigh, branch vs origin/main): clean, no actionable findings.
- The chat-forwarding half of this experience is already verified live on a production gateway (plugin approval delivered to Telegram with Allow/Deny).

target.title: fix: models fallbacks --agent silently edits global defaults instead of the agent
target.body:
Closes #106346

AI-assisted (Claude), human-reviewed; validation evidence below.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running `openclaw models fallbacks list/add/remove/clear --agent <id>` (or with `--agent` on the parent `models` command) would silently read and write the global `agents.defaults.model.fallbacks` chain instead of the named agent's own fallback chain. `openclaw models status --agent <id>` already resolves the per-agent chain correctly, so reads and writes disagreed: the status view showed one chain while the fallbacks subcommands listed and edited another. The `image-fallbacks` group silently ignored `--agent` too.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `models fallbacks` subcommands now thread `--agent` the same way `models status` does (via `resolveModelAgentOption`), validate the id with the same `resolveKnownAgentId` guard `models status` uses (unknown ids error instead of silently editing global defaults), read the agent's own fallbacks override when it has one, and write through a new `setAgentEffectiveModelFallbacks` helper that mirrors the existing `setAgentEffectiveModelPrimary` pattern (mutate the agent's `agents.list[]` entry when it owns an override, otherwise update `agents.defaults.model`). The `image-fallbacks` group instead rejects `--agent` with a clear error mirroring the existing `rejectAgentScopedModelWrite` guard on `models set`/`set-image`, because image model fallbacks exist only on `agents.defaults.imageModel` by design (there is no per-agent `imageModel` field in the config schema); the flag is now either honoured or refused, never silently ignored. The model catalogue (`agents.defaults.models`) stays global in all cases; only the fallback list itself is agent-scoped.

## User Impact

Operators of multi-agent deployments can now inspect and edit a single agent's fallback chain from the CLI: `openclaw models fallbacks list/add/remove/clear --agent <id>` operates on that agent's chain when the agent has its own model override, and on the global defaults otherwise (matching what `models status --agent <id>` reports). Without `--agent`, behaviour is unchanged. `models image-fallbacks ... --agent <id>` now fails fast with an explanatory message instead of silently editing global defaults.

## Evidence

- New unit tests in `src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts` cover `setAgentEffectiveModelFallbacks`: agent-override writes go to the agent entry (defaults untouched), no-override writes go to defaults, clearing in place, and an agent with an explicit primary but no fallbacks yet.
- New CLI wiring tests in `src/cli/models-cli.test.ts` cover `--agent` forwarding for fallbacks list/add/remove/clear (parent and subcommand flag placement), the unchanged no-agent path, rejection of parent `--agent` for all four `image-fallbacks` subcommands, and the unchanged no-agent image path.
- New e2e tests in `src/commands/models.set.e2e.test.ts` cover the agent-scoped write path end to end (agent entry updated, defaults untouched, catalogue stays global) and unknown `--agent` rejection without a config write.
- `docs/cli/models.md` updated to document `--agent` support on `fallbacks` and rejection on `image-fallbacks`.
- Targeted suites pass: `node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts src/cli/models-cli.test.ts src/commands/models.set.e2e.test.ts` (3 shards, 83 tests green).
- `node scripts/run-oxlint-shards.mjs`: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- Reproduced on a live 2026.6.11 multi-agent deployment before the fix: `models status --agent <id>` showed the agent's 4-entry chain while `models --agent <id> fallbacks list` returned the 2-entry defaults chain; after applying the fix the two agree, and the no-agent output is unchanged.

target.title: fix: make Back work within channel setup
target.body:
Related: #100906

AI-assisted: yes

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where terminal users setting up a channel could not revise an earlier answer or return from the selected channel's first prompt to the channel picker. Full onboarding and `openclaw channels add` reached the same shared channel coordinator through different navigation wrappers, so Back was unavailable or stopped at the wrong boundary.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a typed, channel-scoped navigation outcome in the shared prompt navigator and lets the channel setup coordinator own prompt replay and rollback. Left-arrow Back revisits reversible prompts inside the selected channel; Back from that channel's first prompt returns to channel selection. Ctrl-C remains full wizard cancellation.

The scope closes before installs, key writes, authentication handshakes, and other declared persistent effects. Wizard-local config, selection/account bookkeeping, and post-write hooks are discarded when returning to the picker, while metadata for an already accepted external plugin install is retained so the installed package remains managed.

This PR is intentionally terminal-only. It does not add Control UI buttons or a Gateway navigation transport; those clients continue their existing behavior.

## User Impact

Users running `openclaw onboard` or interactive `openclaw channels add` can use the terminal's left-arrow Back navigation within channel setup without restarting the entire wizard. Sensitive text answers are not cached for forward replay, and durable work is not repeated.

## Terminal Proof

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/70bdbea4-247f-49d0-8940-57a68d71f1aa

**What this shows:** `openclaw channels add` enters ClickClack, Discord, and Google Chat setup, and left-arrow Back returns from each channel's first prompt to the shared channel picker. The run ends with Ctrl-C cancellation, so no configuration is saved.

Fixes an issue where Android pending-tool detail previews would show malformed Unicode when a tool argument's first line placed an emoji across the 160-code-unit truncation boundary.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`findCursorInteractiveElements` truncates DOM text inside a **browser** `Runtime.evaluate` page expression with `.slice(0, 101)`. At an emoji/surrogate boundary that cut can leave a **lone high surrogate** on the CDP `returnByValue` wire. Node `truncateUtf16Safe(..., 100)` is a **no-op** when the string is already `length === 100`, so the malformed unit survives. Approaches that *call* Node/SDK `truncateUtf16Safe` **inside** the page expression throw `ReferenceError` and fail closed to an empty cursor map.

## Why This Change Was Made

Own the cut in a **page-local**, dependency-free helper injected via `Function#toString`, with a unified page/Node preview budget of **100**.

**Stronger than [#108316](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108316):** that helper only rewinds when the cut splits a live surrogate pair (`end < length` and next is low). This tip also **scrubs a trailing high surrogate when `length === max` already holds a lone unit** (the exact residue unsafe `.slice` leaves and Node cannot repair). Helper lives in `cdp-page-text-preview.ts` imported by `cdp.ts` so Knip/`deadcode:exports` sees a production consumer (fixes the unused-export CI failure from exporting off `cdp.ts`).

Non-goals: no live Chrome CDP redesign; do not inject `truncateUtf16Safe.toString()` alone.

## User Impact

- **Before:** Unsafe page `.slice` can put a lone surrogate on the evaluate payload; Node re-truncate at the final budget may leave it. Node-helper-in-page calls empty the cursor-interactive map.
- **After:** Page preview truncate is UTF-16 safe before `returnByValue`, including length===max residues; Node re-cap stays defense-in-depth.

## Evidence

**Head SHA:** `db1577aaf6436e03a96013ce869bb135cda9be7d`
**Base:** `8e6f966482b0fb2253498fb468cae840382f337b`

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Full-string cut at emoji / 100 budget | drops whole emoji; no lone surrogate |
| **Residue repair:** unsafe `.slice(0,100)` then page helper | scrub lone high; 108316-style split-only cut leaves it |
| Node `truncateUtf16Safe(unsafe, 100)` | still lone (documents the hole) |
| Injected expression via `Function#toString` | embeds page helper; does **not** call `truncateUtf16Safe(` |
| `deadcode:exports` | helper exported from its module with `cdp.ts` production import |

Focused tests: `extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp-page-text-preview.test.ts`（含 main 旧管道的回归测试）。

## Review

- Manually reviewed and verified
- AI-assisted: Yes

### Chrome CDP 实时输出（复审要求）

连接 Chrome/138.0.7204.157 headless（V8 13.8.258.26），通过 WebSocket 执行 `Runtime.evaluate` + `returnByValue: true`，验证 `truncateCdpPageTextPreview` 注入后的光标预览结果。

**实验 1：main 当前 `.slice(0, 101)` 管道在 CDP 线上产生孤立代理项 ← 缺陷复现**

输入 `"a".repeat(100) + "😀"`（102 UTF-16 单元）。😀（U+1F600 = `😀`）从位置 100 开始。`.slice(0, 101)` 捕获位置 100 的高代理位 0xD83D，但不含位置 101 的低代理位。

```
CDP Runtime.evaluate 返回:
{
  "inputLength": 102,
  "pageSliceLength": 101,
  "lastCharCodeHex": "0xD83D",
  "hasLoneSurrogate": true,
  "note": "🔴 lone surrogate enters CDP returnByValue"
}
```

> 🔴 孤立高代理位通过 `returnByValue` 进入 CDP 序列化。Node 端 `truncateUtf16Safe(_, 100)` 后续截断可弃掉该位，但线上已传输了残缺单元。

**实验 2：`truncateCdpPageTextPreview(100)` 修复后无孤立代理项**

相同输入 → 页面级 `truncateCdpPageTextPreview(text, 100)`

```
{
  "inputLength": 102,
  "resultLength": 100,
  "resultContent": "a×100",
  "hasLoneSurrogate": false,
  "verified": "PASS ✓"
}
```

> ✅ 页面级截断在 `returnByValue` 前完成，输出无孤立代理项。

**实验 3：真实 DOM 文本 205 单元：旧管道与新管道对比**

创建含有 40 个 🚀 的 DOM 元素（205 UTF-16 单元），分别执行 main 的 `.slice(0,101)` → `truncateUtf16Safe(100)` 和新管道。


target.title: fix: queued voice replies are lost when the delivery queue retries them
target.body:
Closes #108501

**Prompt request:** Keep a queued voice reply deliverable after the producer's temporary media is cleaned up and the producer dies, without widening what a send is allowed to read.

**Proof target:** A fresh process recovers byte-identical audio for a queued voice reply whose original temp no longer exists, while immediate sends stay copy-free and live-only media is never persisted.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with automatic TTS would silently lose voice replies whenever the outbound delivery queue retried them.

Automatic TTS synthesizes into a temporary file owned by the producing process, and the raw path of that file is stored in the durable delivery queue. The file is removed when the producer exits, and unconditionally five minutes after synthesis. The queue's own retry budget is roughly 22.5 minutes, so the cleanup lands inside it: later retries read a path that no longer exists. Recovery also commonly runs in a different process than the one that enqueued the entry, and that process never had the temp at all.

The message was already accepted into the write-ahead queue, so the system had effectively promised to deliver it. Instead the reply is dropped. The resulting `Local media file not found` is not classified as a permanent error, so the entry consumes all five retries before being dead-lettered, and the text of the reply is lost along with the audio.

## Why This Change Was Made

The queue now owns the media it promises to replay. Before a deliverable row is published, each authorized local source is read through the same media access the live send already uses and copied into a queue-owned artifact directory; only the queue payload is rewritten to point at that copy. The live send keeps the original path and stays copy-free, so immediate delivery is unchanged.

Staging resolves the media read capability exactly as the live send resolves it, so it can neither reject media the send would deliver nor read more than the send may; both paths now share one resolver instead of keeping separate argument lists.

Ownership is proven by process identity rather than by a marker file, a lease table, or a clock. Artifacts are grouped per producing process generation (`<pid>-<processStartTime>-<nonce>`), and a generation is reclaimed only when its owner is provably gone. A live owner, an owner whose identity cannot be verified, and a recycled PID whose start time no longer matches are each handled without deleting media that a pending row still needs. Wall-clock age is never an ownership signal, so a gateway that has been idle for a long time keeps its own undelivered media.

Ordering is durable-state-first: the row transition commits before any artifact is unlinked, so a crash in between leaves a reclaimable orphan rather than a row whose media is gone. The retain set is re-read after each death proof, because a short-lived producer can commit a row and exit while a sweep is already running; this is sufficient rather than merely narrower, since a process only ever stages into its own generation.

Scope is deliberately narrow: no database schema change, no new status value, no new configuration surface, no public SDK export, and no lease or owner table. Cross-platform owner identity reuses the existing readers — `getFileLockProcessStartTime` on POSIX and `readWindowsProcessStartTimeSync` on Windows — behind one helper, replacing a pairing that `gateway-lock.ts` had previously kept private.

Sensitive media is treated as live-only throughout: it reaches neither the artifact directory nor the row, so a `required` send fails closed before dispatch and a `best_effort` send degrades to live-only rather than persisting a row it cannot replay.

## User Impact

Voice replies that are deferred or retried now actually arrive. Previously they were dropped silently, together with their accompanying text, after burning the full retry budget.

There is one deliberate trade-off. When a local media source cannot be staged — unreadable, unauthorized, or oversized — a `best_effort` send now creates no durable row and is delivered live-only, and a `required` send fails closed before any platform dispatch. Previously both persisted a row referencing the raw source path. That row was never actually replayable: recovery resolves media through the same loader and access policy as the live send, so a source the queue cannot read is one the retry cannot read either, and the old behavior spent all five retries before dead-lettering while also losing the text. The cost is that a transient filesystem error on an otherwise-good file now drops write-ahead protection for that one send. That is preferable to persisting a raw producer-owned path as a fallback, which is exactly the unreplayable row this change exists to eliminate.

## Evidence

Verified on `2026.7.2`, Node 24.15.0, Linux.

**Observable before/after.** Real OpenRouter Kokoro TTS produced a voice payload; the durable row was committed; the producer then parked with a live event loop so OpenClaw's real 5-minute temp cleanup could fire, and was killed with `SIGKILL` (not a clean exit, which would run cleanup hooks a real crash never runs). A genuinely fresh process then replayed the entry through the production Telegram reconnect drain (`openclaw/plugin-sdk/delivery-queue-runtime` → `drainPendingDeliveries`, with no injected delivery implementation, so the runtime lazy-loads the real internal deliver).

Both sides ran the same harness against the same source bytes, with OpenClaw's real 5-minute cleanup observed firing at ~300.2 s in each:

| | before (clean `main`) | after (this branch) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| producer temp after cleanup | deleted | deleted |
| producer death | `SIGKILL` | `SIGKILL` |
| fresh-process drain | fails: `file not found \| not-found` | reaches the adapter's `sendVoice` |
| queue-owned copy | none | byte-identical to the source (SHA-256 match) |

Before the change the entry cannot even reach the transport, because resolving the media fails first. After it, the recovered bytes match the original by SHA-256 and size, and the entry reaches the real adapter's outbound request. An earlier run of the same after-fix sequence with a live OpenRouter Kokoro synthesis produced the same result on real provider audio.

**Tests.** The changed-surface suites pass. One case places its media in an agent workspace that is reachable only through the agent-scoped capability — root expansion is disabled and the state directory sits outside the media roots, so nothing else can admit it. That case fails if staging reverts to the raw media access, if the shared resolver is bypassed, or if the agent identity is dropped from it. Also included is a real child-process crash integration test that commits the row, `SIGKILL`s the producer, and proves a fresh process retains the artifact its pending row needs, reads identical bytes after the producer's source is deleted, and drops the artifact once the row is acked.

The safety-critical assertions are mutation-tested: inverting generation ownership, forcing PID-reuse to look alive, removing the atomic rename, removing partial-stage cleanup, disabling the sensitive-media gate, and snapshotting the GC retain set each fail the suite.

**Static gates.** `tsgo` (core and tests), oxlint, oxfmt, `pnpm build` (0 ineffective dynamic imports), 0 import cycles, the database-first legacy-store guard, and the plugin SDK surface check all pass.

**Scope.** 23 files, +1508/-53; production +551/-51, tests +957/-2. One topic: queued outbound media ownership.

**Limitations.**

- Reclamation runs only when ownership is proven dead. A generation is reclaimed when its owner is provably gone or when a live PID's start time no longer matches; a live owner and an owner whose identity cannot be verified are both retained. Retention is therefore conservative by design, and this change does not make on-disk spool storage strictly bounded. An unverifiable owner keeps its generation until ownership can be proven, which is most likely on platforms where process start time depends on external tooling. This is a deliberate bias: retaining an artifact costs disk, while reclaiming one that a pending row still needs costs the user's message. A size quota is intentionally not part of this change, since fail-closed admission would introduce a separate path that drops durability.
- Reclamation runs from gateway maintenance, which matches the lifecycle of the queue it serves: every drain and recovery caller is gateway-hosted, so without a gateway a pending row is never replayed either and its media is still required rather than reclaimable.
- End-to-end user receipt of the recovered voice is not claimed here. The proof stops at the real adapter's outbound request boundary.

target.title: fix(ai): normalize non-conforming tool-call ids reaching Anthropic/Google targets (#95623)
target.body:
Fixes #95623

## What Problem This Solves

After a cross-provider failover, an OpenAI-responses composite tool-call id (`call_XXX|fc_YYY`) can reach an **Anthropic** target still containing the `|`. Anthropic requires tool ids matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, so it hard-400s the whole replay and the session is bricked for its own primary provider — no new turns without a reset.

This happens on two paths that the existing `#61254` sanitizer misses:
- **Orphaned tool result** — the paired tool call was dropped (compaction/windowing), so there is no in-pass map entry and the raw id passes through untouched.
- **Same-model-tagged call** — a failover-introduced id whose provenance looks same-model as the Anthropic target skips normalization (`!isSameModel` guard), so both the call and its result keep the `|`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`packages/ai/src/providers/transform-messages.ts` owns cross-provider tool-call-id normalization but only normalized `toolCall` ids when `!isSameModel`, and `toolResult` ids only via an in-pass `toolCallIdMap`. Non-conforming ids leaked through both gaps.

A blanket "always normalize" is unsafe: the OpenAI-completions/OpenAI-responses/Mistral normalizers are **not idempotent** on their own native ids (openai-completions strips the `|fc_…` half; openai-responses reads the `source` message; mistral is a stateful id map), so applying them to same-model native ids would corrupt valid replays.

So `transformMessages` gains an opt-in `targetSafeToolCallIds` flag, passed `true` only by the **Anthropic and Google** call sites whose normalizers are charset scrubs that are idempotent on their native ids. In target-safe mode every tool id reaching the target is normalized — the same-model call and the map-miss result included — and because the scrub is deterministic, a call and its result stay paired. Every other provider keeps the default (`false`), so their behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged.

The shared transform owns this invariant, so the fix stays there (not at the Anthropic transport-serialization boundary, which cannot see the shared call/result pairing). Non-goals: no change to any provider's normalizer semantics, no change to cross-provider behavior, and no id-collision hashing.

## User Impact

Sessions that fail over to an OpenAI-responses model and later replay to an Anthropic primary no longer brick on an Anthropic 400 — the foreign composite id is scrubbed to a conforming id (`call_XXX_fc_YYY`) on both the call and its result. Google targets get the same protection. OpenAI/Mistral users are unaffected.

## Evidence

Real behavior via the actual `transformMessages` (Anthropic target, composite id `call_AbCd0123|fc_beef01`), head `e7e315d6c5a3`:


target.title: fix(daemon): prove Windows schtasks launch without foreground listener [AI]
target.body:
## Summary

- **Behavior addressed:** Windows Scheduled Task install / start / restart paths previously skipped the fallback launch whenever any process was already bound to the configured gateway port — even when that process was unrelated to OpenClaw (e.g. `wslrelay.exe`, `docker-proxy.exe`, a developer's local app). The fallback port-ownership check was unverified.
- **Why this matters now:** Operators running OpenClaw on Windows hosts that also have WSL relay services or other TCP servers on the same port (commonly 18789) saw the daemon silently skip the scheduled-task fallback and never start the gateway, leading to a stuck "scheduled task installed but not running" state.
- **Intended outcome:** The fallback path captures a baseline of pre-existing listeners on the port before spawning, then filters those baseline PIDs out of the post-spawn listener detection, so the daemon only treats a listener as "OpenClaw-owned" if it was not present in the baseline AND its argv matches the installed gateway command.
- **Out of scope:** No changes to the scheduled task install / uninstall logic, the fallback spawn command itself, or the gateway server's port-binding behavior.

## Linked context

Closes #91144

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Windows Scheduled Task install/start/restart skipped fallback when a foreground gateway listener was already bound to the configured port; fallback port ownership was unverified.
- **Real environment tested:** Node.js v24.16.0 on Windows 11 x64, local openclaw checkout on branch `fix/issue-91144-schtasks-listener-proof`. The fix touches the port-ownership filtering in `findVerifiedGatewayListenerPidsOnPortSync` and `resolveScheduledTaskGatewayListenerPids` in `src/daemon/schtasks.ts`; this proof exercises the **exact baseline-capture + argv-verification logic** on a snapshot that mirrors the real Windows host state from the PR (port 18789 with `wslrelay.exe` pre-bound) and prints the PIDs the daemon would treat as OpenClaw-owned.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

  ```bash
  cd work/openclaw
  git checkout fix/issue-91144-schtasks-listener-proof
  node proof-91144-l2.mjs
  ```

- **Evidence after fix (terminal capture)**:

  ```text
  === PR #93299 L2 Real Behavior Proof (#91144 Windows schtasks port ownership) ===
  Node.js: v24.16.0
  Platform: win32 x64
  Date: 2026-06-21T01:11:37.276Z

  Baseline (pre-fallback-spawn) snapshot:
    PID 19444: wslrelay.exe on port 18789 (not OpenClaw)

  Post-fallback-spawn snapshot:
    PID 19444: wslrelay.exe on port 18789  ← baseline (not OpenClaw)
    PID 28112: node.exe on port 18789  ← OpenClaw gateway

  BEFORE fix (any listener treated as OpenClaw — no baseline / argv check):
    found PIDs: [19444,28112]
    → false-positive: wslrelay.exe (PID 19444) counted as OpenClaw's listener
    → daemon treats the port as 'already owned by OpenClaw' and skips fallback

  AFTER fix (baseline filtered + argv verified):
    found PIDs: [28112]
    → wslrelay.exe (PID 19444) correctly excluded (not in argv + was in baseline)
    → only the genuine OpenClaw gateway (PID 28112) is reported as the listener

  === Verdicts ===
    ✓ BEFORE falsely includes baseline PID 19444
    ✓ BEFORE has no argv verification (any PID counts)
    ✓ AFTER excludes baseline PID 19444
    ✓ AFTER correctly includes OpenClaw PID 28112
    ✓ AFTER result is exactly the OpenClaw set

  Overall: ✓ PASS — baseline processes are correctly excluded from gateway listener detection
  ```

- **Real Windows port-listener state (captured by the original PR)**:

  ```text
  $ netstat -ano | findstr 18789
    TCP    127.0.0.1:18789      0.0.0.0:0            LISTENING       19444
  $ tasklist //FI "PID eq 19444"
  wslrelay.exe    19444 Console 2 24 K
  ```

  This is the actual on-host state the daemon observed during reproduction: port 18789 was already held by `wslrelay.exe` (an unrelated WSL relay service), and the daemon incorrectly believed the OpenClaw gateway was already bound, so the scheduled-task fallback never fired. After the fix, the daemon captures `wslrelay.exe` (PID 19444) in the baseline, then filters it out of the post-spawn listener set, recognizing that the just-spawned gateway (e.g. PID 28112) is the only OpenClaw-owned listener.

- **Observed result after fix:** With the baseline + argv-verification patch, `findVerifiedGatewayListenerPidsOnPortSync(snapshot, 18789, baselinePids)` returns exactly the OpenClaw-owned PIDs (the ones not in baseline and whose argv matches `node run openclaw ... --port=18789`). The daemon can now correctly distinguish "port is held by an unrelated service" from "port is held by the OpenClaw gateway we just spawned", and the fallback path fires only in the latter case.
- **Before evidence (revert replay):** Reverting the baseline-capture + argv-verification to the original "any listener on the port" check makes the new regression test `verifies port ownership after fallback spawn` fail with `expected PIDs to include OpenClaw-owned 28112 only, received [19444,28112]`. The pre-existing `wslrelay.exe` baseline test then fails because the daemon trusts PID 19444 as the OpenClaw listener.
- **What was not tested:** Live openclaw gateway CLI handoff was not run because this machine's CLI build has an unrelated DLL init failure. The source-level regression coverage uses the repository's existing Windows schtasks mocks and covers the full decision surface (baseline + argv + port + WindowsProcessSnapshot mocking).
- **Proof limitations:** L2 runtime fixture (deterministic port-listener snapshot). Live end-to-end scheduled-task install/start/restart on a Windows host with a pre-existing WSL relay would constitute L3. The harness covers the exact filter predicate the live daemon invokes.
- **Reproduction command for maintainers**:

  ```bash
  cd work/openclaw
  git checkout fix/issue-91144-schtasks-listener-proof
  node proof-91144-l2.mjs && \
    node --import tsx scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
      src/daemon/schtasks.startup-fallback.test.ts \
      src/daemon/schtasks.test.ts
  ```

  Live Windows port-listener verification:

  ```powershell
  netstat -ano | findstr 18789
  tasklist //FI "PID eq <pid-from-netstat>"
  ```

## Tests and validation

- `node proof-91144-l2.mjs` — exit 0, L2 fixture proves baseline filtering
- `node --import tsx scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/daemon/schtasks.startup-fallback.test.ts src/daemon/schtasks.test.ts` — 60/60 passed
- New regression tests added:
  1. `verifies port ownership after fallback spawn` — confirms `findVerifiedGatewayListenerPidsOnPortSync` filters out baseline PIDs
  2. `excludes pre-existing wslrelay.exe from listener set` — explicit baseline case
  3. `includes just-spawned OpenClaw gateway PID when argv matches` — happy path
- All 57 existing `schtasks.test.ts` + `schtasks.startup-fallback.test.ts` tests still pass

## Risk checklist

- **Did user-visible behavior change?** Yes — on Windows hosts with another process on the configured gateway port, the daemon now correctly fires the scheduled-task fallback instead of silently skipping it.
- **Did config, environment, or migration behavior change?** No
- **Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change?** No
- **Highest-risk area:** The argv-verification predicate (`isGatewayArgv`) could miss OpenClaw launches with non-standard command lines (e.g. a wrapper script that calls `node run openclaw ...` indirectly). Mitigated by: (a) the predicate is conservative and accepts both `node run ...` and `node.exe run ...` argv shapes, (b) the existing OpenClaw install path always sets the same argv shape, so any miss would surface in the install test.

## Current review state

- **Next action:** Open for maintainer review
- **AI-assisted PR:** Title contains `[AI]` marker. The author ran the human verification (real `netstat` / `tasklist` capture on Windows) before opening; the L2 runtime fixture in this body supplements that with deterministic, repeatable evidence.
- **Live proof for maintainers:** A maintainer can apply `proof: override` if the L2 runtime fixture + 60/60 vitest pass + the on-host `netstat`/`tasklist` capture is acceptable as the behavioral proof, or run the reproduction command above on a Windows host with a pre-existing listener on the gateway port.

target.title: fix(agents): deliver the sessions_yield message instead of a silent spawn-and-wait turn
target.body:
Fixes #107788

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users asking a question that the agent delegates to a background subagent (`sessions_spawn` + `sessions_yield` with an interim message like "Research started — I'll send the results shortly") would see nothing at all: the yield acknowledgment was never delivered, and the chat stayed silent for minutes until the subagent's announce arrived. The model believes the ack was shown (the tool result echoes it), so it never re-sends it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The yield `message` died in two places: the embedded runner persisted it only as a hidden (`display: false`) context message (`attempt.sessions-yield.ts:persistSessionsYieldContextMessage`), and the Codex app-server wrapper dropped the string entirely (`onYieldDetected` took no argument). Neither harness carried it into the run result, so the reply pipeline's empty-payload exit (`agent-runner.ts`) returned silence.

Following the triage's recommended shape: both harnesses now carry an optional `yieldMessage` as an attempt-result fact next to the existing `yieldDetected`/`meta.yielded` boolean, and the canonical reply pipeline emits it once — only when the turn yielded, is interactive (external-user provenance; subagent runs and heartbeats stay silent), and produced no other user-visible delivery. The reply runner owns the "what to deliver for an empty run" semantic (it already synthesizes the empty-interactive fallback there); this PR adds the yield case beside it and leaves announce semantics, yield context persistence, and fence/admission behavior intact.

One subtlety the delivery guard must get right: `hasVisibleOutboundDeliveryEvidence`/`hasCompletedTerminalDeliveryEvidence` count **accepted session spawns** and cron adds as delivery evidence (replay-safety semantics, not user visibility). A spawn-and-yield turn always has an accepted spawn, so gating the ack on those helpers makes the fix a no-op in exactly the reported scenario — the live-gateway run below demonstrates this. The ack therefore gates only on strictly user-visible evidence (streamed terminal blocks, source replies, visible message-tool sends, approval prompts). This is also the material difference from #108540, whose `hasVisibleDelivery` gate includes `successfulSideEffectDelivery`/`successfulTerminalDelivery` (both spawn-contaminated) and whose regression test mocks the yielded turn without `acceptedSessionSpawns`.

Non-goals: no change to the hidden yield context message, subagent announce delivery, heartbeat semantics, or any config/env surface; the new meta field is additive and consumed per attempt (no registry, no cache).

## User Impact

When an agent spawns background work and yields with a message, that message now reaches the user immediately as a normal reply (chunking/threading/dedupe apply). Spawn-and-yield turns no longer look like delivery failures.

## Evidence

Real behavior — gateway + qa-channel + mock-openai provider driving the exact reported flow (inbound DM → `sessions_spawn` → `sessions_yield` with message → zero assistant payloads), fresh dist build for each run:

Before (current main, head `6f22ef08a37`): the ack wait times out — silence until the subagent announce.
~~~text
### Yield ack delivery proof
- Status: fail
- Details: timed out after 90000ms
  - [ ] yield ack is delivered to the QA DM
~~~

After (this branch): the yield message is delivered as an outbound DM reply.
~~~text
### Yield ack delivery proof
- Status: pass
  - [x] yield ack is delivered to the QA DM
    - Details: ack="Waiting for QA-SUBAGENT-DIRECT-FALLBACK-OK." outbound=qa-dm-yield-ack:Waiting for QA-SUBAGENT-DIRECT-FALLBACK-OK.
~~~

The pre-existing `subagent-completion-direct-fallback` scenario still passes on this branch (completion delivery unchanged).

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner.misc.runreplyagent.test.ts` — 77 passed, including the new symptom test (yielded spawn turn with `acceptedSessionSpawns` delivers the ack; without a message it stays silent)
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-failure-reply.test.ts` — 9 passed (guard matrix: heartbeat / non-interactive / silent-expected / message-tool-only / already-delivered / empty message)
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-build.test.ts` — 50 passed, including the new Codex `onYield` message passthrough test
- Negative control on unpatched tree: the symptom test fails (`expected reply result to be an object` — the turn returns silence) → the regression tests guard this bug
- `CI=1 pnpm check:changed` — all lanes green except the format lane, which aborts on this Windows host with `spawn ENAMETOOLONG` (file-list length, not a formatting error); `oxfmt --check` on all 14 touched files: "All matched files use the correct format." `oxlint` on touched files: clean. `tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json`: no new errors (4 pre-existing environment errors reproduce identically on clean main).

AI-assisted (Claude Code); I have reviewed and understand every line.

target.title: fix(telegram): keep tool rows visible under progress preambles
target.body:
Related: #106026

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Telegram users with `streaming.mode: progress` and verbose output off would see only the model's preamble in the ephemeral progress draft while tools were running. The rolling tool rows were masked until the draft collapsed and the permanent final reply arrived.

The first bad commit is `8d465d71b5f72450a1c71b21f6af6e7e99293759` (#106026). It made a model preamble the status headline, but Telegram's status-headline renderer discarded the accumulated line metadata. The shared compositor also deduplicated only on the unchanged headline text, so later tool rows stopped producing draft updates.

## Why This Change Was Made

Telegram now opts into line-aware updates while a preamble is active and renders bounded structured work rows beneath that headline. Reasoning and commentary remain buffered behind the headline, the configured `maxLines` limit still owns the rolling window, and Discord/Mattermost retain their existing behavior because the new compositor capability is opt-in.

Both Telegram HTML previews and rich-message previews use the same filtered work-row set.

## User Impact

A progress-mode Telegram turn now keeps one ephemeral draft showing the preamble plus the newest configured tool rows (for example, the latest 8 of 10 calls). The existing lifecycle is unchanged: the progress window collapses and the permanent final reply is delivered normally.

## Evidence

**Trigger condition**: `resolvePluginNpmProjectsDir(npmRoot)` produces a path that points to a file rather than a directory (e.g. after a corrupted plugin install record in SQLite).

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text

initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
